title: Nanded, 1708: the Guru is the Granth
hookLine: before he dies the Guru tells the Sikhs that the scripture is now their Guru
carry: the book is the guru now

lines: WHO DO WE GO TO NOW?
cards: When the one who holds a family together is gone, who decides? Who do we go to? From Guru Nanak on, the Sikhs had an answer: the next Guru.
Nanak chose Angad. Angad chose Amar Das. Nine times the light was handed on, person to person.
Now it's 1708. Guru Gobind Singh is far from Punjab, at Nanded on the Godavari river, in the south of India. He is wounded, and he knows he is dying.
His four sons are gone. Everyone waits for the name. The answer is not a person.

teach.b: Guru Granth Sahib. Guru, often explained as the one who leads from darkness to light. Granth, a book.
Sahib, a word of respect, like lord or master. Here's what happened, as Sikhs tell it. At Nanded, an assassin stabbed the Guru.
The wound was stitched, then tore open again.

Before he died, in October 1708, he gathered the Sikhs and bowed before the scripture: the Adi Granth that Guru Arjan had compiled, the one you met on day sixty-two, with the hymns of Guru Tegh Bahadur now added.
After him, he told them, there would be no more human Gurus. The Word in this book was their Guru, and the authority of the community, the Khalsa gathered together, would stand alongside it.
Sikhs call these two the Guru Granth and the Guru Panth. It was a bold step. Nobody could inherit it, buy it, or fight over it.

The Guru is now the same for everyone, and it speaks in the hymns of the Gurus and of saints from other backgrounds too. That's why a gurdwara looks the way it does. The Granth sits on a raised throne under a canopy.
Someone waves a whisk over it, the way you would for a king. In many gurdwaras, at night it's carried to its own room to rest, and brought out again at dawn.
It's treated the way you'd treat a living teacher, because that's what Sikhs say it is.

teach.h: THE BOOK IS THE GURU NOW.
teach.b: And after every Ardas, many congregations sing a couplet that says it plainly: all Sikhs are commanded to accept the Granth as the Guru.

how: In every gurdwara the Guru Granth Sahib is installed each morning on a raised throne under a canopy and put to rest at night, and a daily hukamnama, a line chosen by opening it at random, is read out as the Guru's word for the day.

o: a book of laws from the Mughal court
the scripture Sikhs honor as their living Guru
a written history of the ten Gurus' lives

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the one who leads from darkness to light
where the Granth was named Guru

s: Guru Gobind Singh named his successor from among his followers
he named no person. the scripture became the Guru, with the Khalsa community alongside it.
the Granth is put to rest at night and brought out at dawn
it is treated as a living teacher, not a book on a shelf.
the Granth contains only the words of the Sikh Gurus
it also holds hymns by saints from other backgrounds.

games.q: you're the tenth Guru at Nanded. your sons are gone, and the Sikhs are waiting for the name of the next Guru. what do you do?
o: bow before the scripture and name it the Guru.
leave the choice to a council after you're gone.
games.why: he bowed before the Granth and told the Sikhs that the Word was now their Guru, with the Khalsa, the Guru Panth, alongside it. there would be no more human Gurus.

practice: If you have a gutka, a small prayer book, or the Guru Granth Sahib itself, open it; if not, open a page online, or just picture one: the wide page, the Gurmukhi script.
Rest your eyes on one line, and stay with its meaning if you understand it, or with its shape if you don't. Sikhs say this is how the Guru still speaks: one line, to one person, today.

wordCard.voice: Guru Granth. The Sikh scripture, named by Guru Gobind Singh as the Guru after him, alongside the Guru Panth, the gathered community.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: the Guru, the book, with a word of respect.

carryVoice: Your line: the book is the guru now. A Word for everyone. That's day ninety-three.
